newsitem.title: USA: Investigators hunt links between 3 Atlanta bombings.
newsitem.headline: Investigators hunt links between 3 Atlanta bombings.

text.p: Investigators on Sunday continued their search for links between a bomb that exploded at a lesbian nightclub and two other unsolved bombings that have shaken the city over the past seven months.

A police cordon sealed off streets for several blocks around The Otherside Lounge as agents from the FBI, the U.S. Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF), the Georgia state police and local law enforcement agencies combed through the neighbourhood for pieces of shrapnel and other evidence.

Members of national FBI and ATF response teams arrived from around the country to assist in the investigation of Friday night's blast, and authorities predicted the number of federal agents on the case would reach 100 before Monday.

Late on Saturday, police went on alert once again after an anonymous caller phoned a bomb threat into the city fire station that had responded to the nightclub bombing. A nearby hotel and dozens of businesses were evacuated. But no bomb turned up during the ensuing search.

Officials said the attack was similar to two others in Atlanta -- a January double-bombing at an abortion clinic and the deadly Centennial Olympic Park bombing last July. Those similarities led a senior FBI official to speculate that investigators could be dealing with a serial bomber.

"The bombings have not been categorically tied together yet. Of course, the last bombing was aimed at an abortion clinic. It's a possibility that this one was motivated by hate," said FBI spokesman Jay Spadafore.

The nightclub bomb, apparently packed with nails, went off in the rear patio section of the lounge in northeast Atlanta shortly before 10 p.m. EST (0300 GMT Saturday). Staff said the club, one of Atlanta's few predominantly lesbian bars, was about half full at the time.
Police found a second bomb in a backpack hidden among some bushes in an adjacent parking lot and detonated the device with a remote-control robot.
Both police and nightclub staff said there were no prior warnings and no claims of responsibility for the attack.

"We all recognise that there are similarities here. We will be searching out the possibility that we have a serial bomber," Woody Johnson, the special agent in charge of the Atlanta FBI office, told a news conference.

Of the five people hurt in the blast, only one was seriously injured. She was identified as Memrie Wells-Crestwell of Snellville, Ga. A spokesman for Grady Memorial Hospital said she was listed in stable condition.
Wells-Crestwell, who was initially believed to have been shot, rolled up her sleeve to find a three- to four-inch (eight- to 10-cm) nail sticking through her arm, according to eyewitnesses.

"Whether or not it's a serial bomber, or a copy-cat bomber, it makes no difference," Mayor Bill Campbell said on Sunday morning television. "We must find the person, or persons, who are responsible and stop them before they hurt someone again."
Homosexual rights activists condemned the bombing as a hate crime reminiscent of Ku Klux Klan attacks on blacks in the 1960s and the burning of black churches in recent years.
The National Gay and Lesbian Task Force wrote to President Bill Clinton, pressing him to "speak out loudly" against the attack and calling for a U.S. Justice Department investigation.

Under federal law, the Justice Department can investigate a crime as bias-motivated if it might have been driven by hate against a certain race, religion, national origin or disability. The statutes do not include sexual orientation.

The use of a backpack for the second device resembled the Centennial Olympic Park bombing in July. In that incident, a pipe bomb packed with nails and hidden in a green military-style knapsack exploded during a crowded outdoor concert in downtown Atlanta, leaving two people dead and more than 100 wounded.
